content.thinking:
I don't have actual metrics, logs, or deploy data here—the cause is just a hypothesis around state divergence, confirmed only by the mitigation of removing 90 stale entries. The duration figure is a lower bound, so I need to be careful not to restate given figures as if I'd computed them myself, and I shouldn't invent impact numbers either—I have to flag these as assumptions rather than facts.

Both the onset time and the divergence start are unverified assumptions, not measured data, with the cache flush being the only concrete evidence I actually have. In the summary I should describe things plainly, like the shopping service holding outdated spending totals, rather than naming internal components, and I should note that recovery itself wasn't confirmed by metrics—the mitigation agent just assumed success as soon as it began waiting.

assumptions: The incident's duration is a lower bound, not a measurement: the service had not been observed to recover by the last minute of metrics available, so the real duration may be substantially longer than the window we can account for.
The 20:33 UTC onset was assigned by the investigator despite zero minutes of metrics being returned; it is not derived from observed data.
The claim that divergence began around 17:40 UTC comes from the candidate explanation, not from any retrieved metric, log or change record.
Error rate and user impact are unknown — metrics for the incident could not be read — so no impact figure in this report is measured.

Queries for logs, metrics and production changes all returned empty across several time windows. We treated this as an absence of signal consistent with a silent stale-copy fault, but we cannot rule out that the data sources themselves were not returning results, which would also explain the emptiness.

Confirmation of the mitigation was recorded in the same second the agent began waiting for the service to respond, so 'confirmed' rests on the cache store reporting 90 entries removed rather than on an observed post-fix healthy response.
No deploy, release or feature-flag change was found, so the trigger that caused the cache to stop following the ledger remains unidentified; recurrence cannot be ruled out.
The time Argus held the incident (about 0.01 hours) measures response speed only and says nothing about how long the service was degraded.
input.executive_summary: The shop service kept a saved copy of how much each shopper had spent, and that copy stopped being updated while the underlying record of purchases stayed correct. For a period on 2 October 2026 — beginning at or before 20:33 UTC and continuing past the last data we have, so at least several minutes and possibly far longer — shoppers and anything reading those totals could have been shown out-of-date spend figures. Nothing was unavailable and nothing was slow, which is why the problem surfaced only through a consistency check rather than through failures. Automation picked up the alert, investigated, and discarded the stale saved figures; the storage layer reported 90 entries removed, after which the alert cleared. How many shoppers saw a wrong total, and for how long each was affected, was not measured and cannot be stated. A draft code fix has been opened for review.
input.root_cause: A cache of shopper spend totals (io-summary-cache) stopped tracking the purchase ledger and kept serving stale totals; the ledger itself stayed correct, so no requests failed or slowed and only the alert's reconciliation check detected the divergence. This is the leading explanation rather than a proven one: no metrics, logs, deploys or flag changes were retrievable for the window, and the only direct evidence is that flushing the cache removed 90 stale entries and cleared the alert. Why the cache fell behind in the first place was never established.
